ceviri.26: Which runs faster, React Native or Flutter?
ceviri.27: In everyday use there is no difference a user would notice between the two. On work such as scrolling a list, filling in a form or displaying content, both frameworks run comfortably. The divergence begins on screens that call for heavy animation and continuous redrawing; there, the approach that draws with its own brush behaves more predictably. It wouldn't be right to decide on that difference without measuring it against your own heaviest screen. General claims about speed are usually repeated without ever being measured.

ceviri.31: It is, but don't overstate it. The components don't carry across directly; what carries across is the language, the habits around the tooling and part of the business logic. Even that makes a noticeable difference to the schedule.
ceviri.32: Which one also works on desktop and web?

ceviri.39: There are well-known products using both. But someone else's choice knows nothing about your team's language or your product's expectations of the interface.

ceviri.41: What your team's language is, and whether the interface should resemble the device or the brand. Those two close most of the decision.

ceviri.55: React Native or Flutter? A Single Codebase Comparison
ceviri.56: These two names come up side by side in most meetings, and the discussion quickly turns into taking sides. Yet both are mature, and both carry large products. The right question isn't which is better but which one fits your team and your product. In this article we compare them on four criteria. We aren't giving figures; the comparison runs on criteria.
ceviri.57: Two frameworks doing the same job by different routes: one connects outwards, the other stays within itself.
ceviri.59: What Is the Fundamental Difference Between React Native and Flutter?
ceviri.60: The difference gathers around who draws the screen. React Native bridges to the platform's own components; Flutter draws every pixel itself. The first feels familiar to the device, the second looks exactly the same on both platforms. They diverge on the language side too: one comes from the JavaScript family, the other uses Dart. You make the choice along those two axes.
ceviri.61: We opened up the mechanical difference between a bridging framework and a self-drawing one in detail in the
ceviri.63: article. We aren't repeating that mechanism here; we are looking at where the two frameworks diverge in practice.
ceviri.64: We'll work through four criteria. The order matters: the first settles most of the decision on its own.
ceviri.66: — the developer experience you already have.
ceviri.68: — familiar to the device, or identical everywhere.
ceviri.72: — how often version migrations come, and how painful they are.
ceviri.73: If Both Do the Same Job, Why Is the Choice Hard?
ceviri.74: Because both of them work. The choice isn't a test of competence, it is a question of fit. Because React Native bridges to native components, the interface shows small differences from device to device; Flutter erases those differences entirely. Which of the two you want depends on your product.
ceviri.75: Which Language Does Your Team Command?
ceviri.76: This question comes last on most lists, yet it is the most concrete criterion of all. A team writing JavaScript on the web side makes fast progress with React Native. For a team with Dart experience, or one you are hiring from scratch, Flutter puts nothing in the way. Setting off in a language you don't know grows both the schedule and the maintenance load.
ceviri.77: If you already have a web product, the picture changes. The validation rules, the formatting helpers and part of the business logic are written in the same language. On the React Native side, carrying that experience across is relatively easy.
ceviri.78: On a team built from scratch, the language becomes a preference rather than an obstacle. Learning Dart doesn't take an experienced developer weeks.
ceviri.79: When you choose the team language, think about two years from now rather than today. Who will maintain the app, and which language is that person comfortable in? Keeping a framework standing after the team has dispersed is harder than setting it up. That is why we don't leave the decision to a single developer's preference; we invite the whole team to the table.
ceviri.80: What Does the Hiring Side Look Like?
ceviri.81: There is a pool of candidates on both sides; how easy the search is varies with your city and your salary. That is why we don't answer the question “which one has more developers” without measuring it. Looking at your own hiring history is more reliable than general claims.
ceviri.82: How Does the Interface Look on Each Route?
ceviri.83: On the bridging route, when you press a button a real system button responds. On the self-drawing route, the same brush does the work on every platform. React Native sits closer to the first, Flutter to the second. If you want a uniform brand language, the second suits you. If the habits of the device matter, the first sits better.
ceviri.84: The argument about how a screen looks is usually had over screenshots, yet the difference emerges in motion. Scroll deceleration, keyboard behaviour and the back gesture vary from device to device. A self-drawing framework imitates them itself; the imitation is good, but it isn't exact.
ceviri.85: If you want heavy custom animation and brand-specific motion design, the self-drawing route leaves you more room.
ceviri.86: Don't forget the accessibility side either. Screen reader support, text size settings and contrast come ready in platform components. On the self-drawing route you have to set those up separately; the framework helps, but the work stays with you. If you are building a public sector or enterprise product, this heading is not up for negotiation.
ceviri.87: On Which Side Is a Design System Easier to Build?
ceviri.88: If you are aiming for a uniform look, a self-drawing framework makes the job easier. On the route that leans on platform components, you have to try the same component separately on two devices.
ceviri.89: How Do the Package Ecosystem and the Maintenance Load Diverge?
ceviri.90: There is a wide pool of packages on both sides, but they have different characters. The React Native ecosystem carries the accumulated work of the web world; choice is abundant and quality fluctuates. On the Flutter side, the ready-made libraries are tidier and relatively fewer in number. What determines the maintenance load isn't the number of packages but how regularly the ones you pick are maintained.
ceviri.91: When we choose a package we look at three things: the date of the last update, the number of open issues and the number of maintainers. A package maintained by one person is a risk, however good it is. Those criteria work the same way on both sides.
ceviri.92: Version migrations come into the picture too. A major release once a year is ordinary; the real question is how painful the migration is. The only honest way to measure that is to try it with your own dependency list. Both frameworks have a published release policy;
ceviri.95: Are Fewer Packages Better, or More?
ceviri.96: Neither; the right package is better. Abundant choice creates decision fatigue, while narrow choice sometimes leads you to write your own bridge. On the native side, finding a ready-made solution for React Native is usually easy, but you then have to verify separately that what you found is maintained.
ceviri.97: Keeping the dependency list short is a strategy in itself. Every ready-made library you add is a piece of work waiting for you at the next version migration. Five maintained packages beat twenty orphaned ones. Reviewing the list once a year is a good habit too.
ceviri.98: “Both frameworks work. The question isn't which is better, but which one fits your team.”
ceviri.100: Which Product Should Choose Which Framework?
ceviri.101: Three criteria settle it: team language, expectations of the interface, and the web codebase you already have. A team writing JavaScript and a wish for an interface familiar to the device strengthen the React Native side. A uniform brand language and heavy custom animation bring the Flutter side forward. If the three diverge, the team language carries the most weight.
ceviri.102: There is a tendency by kind of product too. Enterprise dashboards, field applications and content products run comfortably on either side. On products with high visual ambition and dense motion design, the self-drawing framework comes forward.
ceviri.103: Once the choice is settled, the schedule settles too; we set out the stages in the

If you are building from scratch, look at which of the two you find candidates for faster; measure that with your own hiring history. General claims about popularity may not hold in your city. The number you measure is always more accurate than the claim you read.
ceviri.109: Let's Make the Framework Choice Together
ceviri.110: The choice isn't a purely technical preference. We weigh your team's language, your expectations of the interface and the web code you already have, together. What you are left with is not a brand name but the reasoning behind the choice. The difference between React Native and Flutter only takes on meaning through that reasoning. The wrong framework shows itself in the second release.
ceviri.111: In the meeting we tick off the four criteria one by one and write down together which one carries the most weight.
ceviri.115: — both are open if you'd like to look through them.
ceviri.116: We write the decision onto a single page: which criterion pointed which way, which one carried the most weight, and why. Six months on, when somebody asks, the answer is ready. Framework arguments come back around most often because the reasoning was never written down. A written rationale closes that argument once.
ceviri.117: The difference between abundance of choice and tidiness shows itself in the maintenance load.
